header: Stereo. H C J D A 38.
(Dr. Ahsan Abdullah. v. Aazar Ibrahim Siddiqui, etc.)
body: Date of hearing: 04.11.2026 Petitioner by: Sardar Muhammad Ashfaq Abbasi, Advocate.
State by: Mr. Shoukat Rehman Bhatti, DDPP.
Respondents No.2 to 5. Syed Asghar Ali Sherazi, Advocate.

SYED FARHAD ALI SHAH, J.: Through the instant petition for special leave to appeal, filed under Section 417(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (‘Cr.P.C’), Dr. Ahsan Abdullah (‘petitioner’ or ‘petitionercomplainant’) has assailed the vires of order dated 29.06.2026 (‘impugned order’), passed by the learned Sessions Judge/Special Judge, Anti-Corruption, Rawalpindi Division, Rawalpindi (‘trial Court’), whereby present respondents No.1 to 5, namely, Aazar Ibrahim Siddiqui, Safdar Jang, Malik Pervaiz Akhtar, Zaheer Haider and Fazeel Bhatti, were acquitted of the charge framed against them in a private complaint.

2. Brief facts leading to the institution of the present PSLA are that the petitioner instituted a private complaint, alleging therein that following the demise of his father, Muhammad Ismail Siddiqui, respondent No.1, being his real brother, in connivance with the officials of the Excise and Taxation Department, fraudulently procured the transfer of vehicle bearing registration No. RIV-9193 in his own name and, subsequent thereto, in the name of Muhammad Rizwan, through the preparation of forged documents and misuse of official authority by respondents No.2 to 4. The learned trial Court, upon summoning the respondents, proceeded with the trial. During the course of trial proceedings, respondents No.1 to 5 moved separate applications under Section 265-K, Cr.P.C, seeking their acquittal. The learned trial Court, after hearing learned counsel for the parties and PSLA No.39 of 2026 2 examining the material available on record, allowed the said applications and acquitted the respondents through the impugned order.

3. The main contention advanced by the learned counsel for the petitioner is that the respondents, in connivance with one another, fraudulently transferred the vehicle belonging to the deceased father of the petitioner by forging documents and abusing their respective official positions. In support of the said contention, reliance has been placed upon the judgment rendered by the learned Civil Judge 1st Class, Rawalpindi, in a suit for declaration instituted by the petitioner against respondent No.1, the Director General, Excise and Taxation, and others. It is contended that the Civil Court declared the disputed vehicle to be the joint property of the legal heirs and further held that its transfer in favour of respondent No.1 was contrary to law and facts, having been procured through fraud and misrepresentation. On the strength of the said judgment, it is argued that sufficient material was available to proceed against the respondents for the alleged criminal acts.
4. Per contra, the learned DDPP, assisted by the learned counsel for Respondents No.2 to 5, has vehemently opposed the said contention and supported the legality of the impugned order.
5. Arguments heard. Record perused.

6. At the very outset, and before appraising the merits of the respective contentions raised at the bar, it is imperative to briefly reiterate that the jurisdiction vested in the trial Court by Section 265-K, Cr.P.C, is that the said provision empowers the trial Court to acquit an accused at any stage of the proceedings, after hearing the parties and recording reasons in writing in instances where the trial Court finds that there is no probability of the accused being convicted of any offence. The exercise of this statutory power is not circumscribed merely because the accused has been summoned or a formal charge has already been framed. In this regard, reliance is placed upon a case law reported as Niaz Ahmed and another v. Aijaz Ahmed and others (PLD 2024 SC 1152), wherein it was held that: “The bare perusal of the above-provision reveals that law permits the exercise of powers "at any stage of the case" without specifying a particular stage. The words "at any stage" used in both the sections include the stages before or after framing of the charge or after recording of some evidence.”

Further, in a case reported as Abbas Haider Naqvi andother v. Federation of Pakistan and others (PLD 2022 SC 562), the Honourable Supreme Court PSLA No.39 of 2026 3 authoritatively held that Section 265-K, Cr.P.C, empowers the trial Court to acquit an accused at any stage of the case, where, after hearing the parties and recording reasons, it finds that there is no probability of his being convicted of any offence. Such a stage may arise at the very inception of the proceedings, upon taking cognizance and before recording the prosecution evidence or at a subsequent stage, after framing of charge or even after recording of some prosecution evidence. While doing so, it was further held that that ordinarily, an accused seeking acquittal under Section 265-K, Cr.P.C, may invoke one or more of the following grounds to demonstrate that there is no probability of his conviction:

(i) Absence of an offence: Even if the facts alleged by the prosecution are accepted at their face value, they do not constitute the commission of any offence by the accused. [Internal citations: Muhammad Ashraf v. The State (1990 PCr.LJ 347), Muhammad Taqi v. The State (1991 PCr.LJ 963) and Yasin Khan v. The State (1995 PCr.LJ 142).] (ii) Absence of incriminating material: There is no evidence or incriminating material on the record connecting the accused with the commission of the alleged offence. [Internal citations: Abdul Sattar v. The State (1992 PCr.LJ 2054) and Muhammad Sharif v. Muhammad Hussain (1993 PCr.LJ 2053).] (iii) Insufficiency of available material: The evidence or incriminating material collected during investigation and proposed to be produced at trial is insufficient to sustain a conviction; consequently, even if such evidence is formally brought on record, it would not warrant the conviction of the accused for any offence. [Internal citations: Ghafooran v. Muhammad Bashir (1977 SCMR 292), Ghulam Habib v. The State (1980 PCr.LJ 754) and Sheroo Khan v. Kaloo Khan (1992 PCr.LJ 110).] (iv) No likelihood of improvement through remaining evidence:

The prosecution evidence recorded thus far fails to establish a case warranting conviction, and the remaining evidence, even if recorded, would not improve the prosecution case against the accused in any material respect. [Internal citations: Muhammad Sharif v. The State (PLD 1999 SC 1063), The State v. Asif Ali Zardari (1994 SCMR 798) and Din Muhammad v. Muhammad Sharif (1979 PCr.LJ 59).] Thus, the decisive consideration under Section 265-K, Cr.P.C, is not the stage at which the application is moved, but whether, upon an assessment of the material available on record and the remaining evidence proposed to be produced, there exists any probability of the accused being convicted of an offence. Reliance in this regard is also placed on a case reported as Ammad Yousaf v. The State and another (PLD 2024 SC 273).

7. In view of the jurisprudence on the subject, as well as the above principles, I have considered the aforesaid contention of the learned counsel for the petitioner PSLA No.39 of 2026 4 and found the contention so raised at the bar by the learned counsel of the petitioner to be devoid of any merits. There is no cavil with the proposition that the judgment rendered by the Civil Court determined the civil rights of the parties in respect of the disputed vehicle; nevertheless, a finding regarding joint ownership of the vehicle or the illegality of its transfer, even if founded upon fraud and misrepresentation, does not, by itself, establish the criminal culpability of the accused-respondents allegedly involved in the transaction. The nature of civil and criminal proceedings, as well as the standard of proof governing the two jurisdictions, remain altogether distinct. Reliance is placed on cases law reported as Zakaullah Khan v. Muhammad Aslam and another (1991 SCMR 2126) and Salman Ashraf v. Additional District Judge, Lahore and others (2023 SCMR 1292). Therefore, it was incumbent upon the complainant-petitioner to bring on record legally admissible evidence establishing the commission of the alleged offences and, more particularly, the specific role attributable to each of the respondents to establish criminal culpability.

8. At the same time, it is equally trite that Articles 54 to 57 of the Qanun-e- Shahadat Order, 1984 (‘QSO’), deal with the relevancy and evidentiary effect of judgments, orders and decrees of Courts of Justice. Article 54, QSO, makes relevant the existence of a judgment, order or decree which by law prevents a Court from taking cognizance of a suit or holding a trial, where the question is whether that Court ought to do so. It is the evidentiary counterpart of Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (res judicata), and of Section 403, Cr.P.C, read with Article 13 of the Constitution (double jeopardy). Article 55, QSO, concerns final judgments, orders or decrees of a competent Court in probate, matrimonial, admiralty or insolvency jurisdiction which confer or take away a legal character, or declare a person entitled to a legal character or to a specific thing, not against a specified person but absolutely. Such judgments are relevant when that character or title is relevant, and are conclusive proof of the time at which the legal character accrued or ceased, or from which the thing became that person’s property. Such judgments are relevant and constitute conclusive proof of the date on which the legal character was conferred, accrued or ceased to exist, as well as the date from which the property declared to belong to a person became, or was deemed to have become, his property, but such a judgment does not strip away the authority of a subsequent Criminal Court to determine the liability of an accused before it simply by virtue of its existence. This is followed by Article 56, QSO, makes relevant other PSLA No.39 of 2026 5 judgments, orders or decrees which relate to matters of a public nature relevant to the inquiry, but they are not conclusive proof of what they state. A decree concerning a public right of way, or a general custom, is an illustration. Article 57, QSO, provides that judgments, orders or decrees other than those mentioned in Articles 54, 55 and 56, QSO, are irrelevant, unless their existence is a fact in issue or they are relevant under some other provision of the QSO. Article 58, QSO, permits a party to show that a judgment relevant under Articles 54 to 56, QSO, and proved by the adverse party, was delivered by a Court not competent to deliver it or was obtained by fraud or collusion.

9. A conjoint reading of the aforesaid provisions makes it abundantly clear that the evidentiary value of a previous judgment depends on the provision under which it is tendered. Articles 54, 55 and 56, QSO, have no application in the present case because there is no law placing any embargo on the trial Court's jurisdiction to conduct a criminal trial because of a Civil Court’s judgment. It was held by an Honourable 5-Member Bench of the Supreme Court of Pakistan in a case reported as Sheikh Muhammad Naseem v. Mst. Farida Gul (2016 SCMR 1931) that civil and criminal proceedings being independent of each other and go side by side and institution of one is not a bar on the other. Insofar as Article 55, QSO, is concerned, this Article has no application to the Civil Court’s judgment relied upon by the petitioner. The Article operates only where each of its conditions is satisfied: the judgment, order or decree must be final and must be that of a competent Court exercising probate, matrimonial, admiralty or insolvency jurisdiction; it must confer or take away a legal character, or declare a person entitled to a legal character or to a specific thing; and it must do so not as against any specified person but absolutely. Even then, the judgment is relevant only when the existence of that legal character, or the title of that person to that thing, is itself relevant, and it is conclusive proof only of the time at which the legal character accrued or ceased, or from which the thing became that person’s property. None of these conditions are met because the judgment was rendered by a Civil Judge 1st Class in a suit for declaration, that is, in the exercise of ordinary civil jurisdiction, and not in probate, matrimonial, admiralty or insolvency jurisdiction; the declaration concerns the estate of a deceased person does not convert a declaratory suit into proceedings in probate jurisdiction; the question before the trial Court was not the existence of a legal character or title to the vehicle but whether the respondents had committed forgery and misused official authority; any finding by the Civil Court that the transfer was contrary to law is a finding recorded on the evidence in that suit, which PSLA No.39 of 2026 6 cannot be transplanted in another case and the criminal case was to be decided in the light of evidence so produced in the criminal case alone, and Article 55, QSO, only attaches conclusiveness to the matters it enumerates, namely, the time at which a legal character or title accrued or ceased; a finding of fraud is not among them, nor does the judgment determine who prepared the forged documents or who is criminally liable. Simply put, Article 55, QSO, does not displace the duty of the Criminal Court to determine the liability of the accused on the evidence before it. Furthermore, Article 56, QSO, is not applicable because the Civil Court’s judgment does not concern a matter of public nature. The question therefore falls under Article 57, QSO, and the judgment is irrelevant because neither of its two exceptions are attracted. The existence of the judgment is not itself a fact in issue which solely governs criminal liability, and no other provision of the QSO has been pointed out by the learned counsel to make its findings relevant and in any event, a judgment determining the civil rights of the parties cannot, by itself, be treated as a substitute for the evidentiary threshold required to establish criminal liability before a Criminal Court. This legal position was elucidated by the erstwhile Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of Pakistan, namely, Mr. Justice Muhammad Monir, in his book titled The Law of Evidence, in which it has been stated that a judgment of a Civil Court is not admissible in criminal proceedings to establish the truth of the facts upon which it is rendered, as the guilt of an accused person is to be determined exclusively on the basis of evidence brought before the Criminal Court. The aforesaid principle finds support in the judgment of the Privy Council in a case law reported as Kumar Gopika Raman Roy v. Atal Singh (AIR 1929 PC 99), wherein it was held as under:

“The Evidence Act does not make a finding of fact arrived at on the evidence before the Court in one case evidence of that fact in another case.” To the extent of the applicability and binding nature of precedents rendered by the Privy Council, it follows that according to the Government of India Act, 1935, which was passed by the British parliament in 1935 and came into effect in 1937, the law laid down by the Federal Court, and the Privy Council was binding upon all the Courts of the sub-continent of India, and the law laid down remained applicable to the Courts in Pakistan after the partition. The caveat being that postindependence, in instances where there was a conflict between the opinion of the Privy Council and the then-Federal Court, present Supreme Court of Pakistan, the decisions rendered by the latter would prevail on the Courts of the Country. However, it is to be noted that the decisions of the Privy Council, although not PSLA No.39 of 2026 7 binding on Pakistani Courts, remain expositions of law by one of the highest judicial tribunals in the world can be considered as guidelines for the proper exposition of law. Reliance is placed on a case law reported as Noorul Hassan and others v. The Federation Of Pakistan (PLD 1956 FC 331), in which case, it was held that:

“I agree that decisions of the Privy Council are no longer binding on us now, but being expositions of the law by one of the highest judicial tribunals, in the world composed ‑ of distin-guished men who had special knowledge of our public law, they are entitled to the greatest respect and we are not to disregard them merely on the ground of changed conditions because the recognition of any such ground for departure from well‑settled and fundamental principles would be tantamount to imputing judicial dishonesty to that Tribunal.”

The essence of the principle enunciated in Atal Singh (supra) was followed by the Honourable Supreme Court of Pakistan, in a case reported as Mst. Naseer Begum v. Sain and 6 others (1972 SCMR 584), and their lordships refused to accept the argument that a Civil Court judgment should have been taken into consideration while deciding criminal proceedings. The Honourable Supreme Court went on to observe that the Evidence Act, present QSO, does not render a finding of fact arrived at in one judicial proceeding admissible as evidence of that fact in another proceeding. Subsequently, in a case reported as Malik Khuda Bakhsh v. The State (1995 SCMR 1621), the Honourablei Supreme Court of Pakistan once again held that a judgment passed by a Civil Court is not admissible in criminal proceedings to establish the truth of the facts upon which it is rendered. The dictum of Malik Khuda Bakhsh (supra) was followed by this Court in a case reported as Allah Dita v. Additional Sessions Judge, Sheikhupura and 3 others (PLD 2011 Lahore 246), wherein it was observed as under:

“The contention of learned counsel that judgment of the Civil Court will be admissible in criminal proceedings to establish the truth or falsehood of the said criminal case. I am afraid of the fact that this proposition has been dealt with by the honourable apex Court in the case of Malik Khuda Bakhsh v. The State (1995 SCMR 1621) and it was observed that judgment of a Civil Court is not admissible in a criminal proceedings to establish the truth of the facts upon which it is rendered. So, the contention of the learned counsel for the appellant to this effect that proceedings in criminal trial be stayed has no force at all.” Thus, the consistent judicial view based is that a finding recorded by a Civil Court, cannot, merely by virtue of such finding, be treated as evidence of the facts in criminal proceedings, and that the question of criminal liability must be independently determined on the basis of evidence brought before the Criminal Court, and not merely on the basis of the Civil Court judgment.

PSLA No.39 of 2026 8 10. In light of the above deliberation, the judgment of the learned Civil Court, even if it declared the transfer of the disputed vehicle to be fraudulent and unlawful, cannot, by itself, constitute proof of the criminal allegations levelled against the respondents. The criminal liability of each respondent was required to be independently established through legally admissible evidence before the competent Criminal Court. Merely placing reliance upon the findings recorded in the civil proceedings does not suffice to establish the commission of the alleged offences.

11. Furthermore, and irrespective of the above deliberation, the case is even otherwise one of no incriminating material because of the plea taken by respondent No.3, namely, Malik Pervaiz Akhtar. He asserted that he assumed charge as Excise and Taxation Officer, Rawalpindi, on 02.05.2015, whereas the alleged transfer of the vehicle had taken place much earlier, i.e., on 14.01.2011. The complainantpetitioner failed to rebut this assertion through any documentary evidence. Similarly, no material was brought on record to establish that respondents No.2, 4 and 5 were posted against the relevant seats or had any nexus with the transfer proceedings at the material time. Even the official log record was not shown to disclose their participation either in the transfer of the vehicle or its subsequent cancellation. The learned trial Court also took notice of the fact that the Anti- Corruption Establishment had conducted an enquiry into the allegations and recommended that the matter be dropped, as no incriminating material had surfaced against the persons nominated by the complainant-petitioner. Although the outcome of such enquiry cannot, by itself, be regarded as conclusive of the respondents’ innocence, it nevertheless remains a relevant circumstance to be assessed alongside the remaining material on record. The above fact was also put in juxtaposition by the learned trial Court with the contents of the complaint, the cursory statement of the complainant-petitioner and the documents produced by him, marked as Mark-1 to Mark-19. It was observed that documents Mark-1 to Mark-10 were mere photocopies, whereas Mark-11 to Mark-19 comprised attested copies of the proceedings conducted before the Ex-Officio Justice of Peace and the Anti-Corruption Establishment. Neither the original record pertaining to the alleged fraudulent transfer nor any independent evidence demonstrating the respondents’ participation in the transaction was produced. In particular, no original transfer file, movement register, official noting, approval or any other relevant departmental record was brought on record to establish the involvement PSLA No.39 of 2026 9 of the official respondents in the alleged transaction. In the given circumstances, the allegations levelled against the official respondents are bereft of tangible evidentiary support and such absence of incriminating material, or the insufficiency of the material available to sustain a conviction, furnishes a recognised ground for acquittal under Section 265-K, Cr.P.C, as expounded in cases reported as Abbas Haider Naqvi and another v. Federation of Pakistan and others (PLD 2022 SC 562), Ammad Yousaf v. The State and another (PLD 2024 SC 273) and Niaz Ahmed and another v. Aijaz Ahmed and ohters (PLD 2024 SC 1152).

12. It is also a settled principle that an order of acquittal reinforces the presumption of innocence, giving rise to a double presumption in favour of the accused. Consequently, interference by the appellate Court is justified only where the impugned order is found to be perverse, arbitrary, the result of misreading or non-reading of material evidence, or otherwise suffers from a patent illegality. Reliance is placed on cases reported as Ghulam Sikandar v. Mamaraz Khan (PLD 1985 SC 11), The State and others v. Abdul Khaliq and others (PLD 2011 SC 554) and Altaf Yousuf v. The State through Additional Director FIA and another (2026 SCP 210). In the present case, the learned trial Court has recorded cogent and well-founded reasons for concluding that there is no reasonable probability of the respondents’ conviction. The principle is further fortified in a case law reported as Bashir Ahmad v. Additional Sessions Judge, Faisalabad and 4 others (PLD 2010 SC 661), in which case the Honourable Supreme Court upheld an acquittal under Section 265-K, Cr.P.C, in a private complaint, while deprecating the criminalisation of a bona fide civil dispute, holding it to amount to abuse of the process of law. Relevant excerpt is reproduced for ready reference, as under: “the petitioner had tried to transform a bona fide civil dispute between the parties into a criminal case so as to bring the weight of criminal law and process to bear upon respondents Nos. 2 to 4 in order to extract concessions from them. Such utilization of the criminal law and process by the petitioner has been found by us to be an abuse of the process of law which cannot be allowed to be perpetuated.” The present lis appears to be no different and it is palpable from the perusal of the record that the machinery of the criminal justice system was invoked in order to extract concessions on the present respondents, which amounts to abuse of the process of the law.

13. Considering the above, even if the allegations levelled by the petitioner are examined in conjunction with the judgment rendered by the Civil Court, the absence of legally admissible evidence establishing the specific involvement of the PSLA No.39 of 2026 10 respondents in the alleged criminal transaction remains an insurmountable deficiency in the prosecution case, making it a case of no evidence with no probability of conviction. Learned counsel for the petitioner has been unable to identify any misreading or non-reading of material evidence, perversity in the findings, or patent legal infirmity in the impugned order so as to warrant interference by this Court with the impugned judgment.

14. In wake of the above, I am of the considered view that the learned trial Court has rightly exercised its jurisdiction under Section 265-K, Cr.P.C, and the impugned order is founded upon sound reasoning, suffering from no illegality, perversity or material infirmity warranting interference by this Court. Consequently, finding no merit in the instant petition, the same is dismissed, and the impugned order dated 29.06.2026, passed by the learned Sessions Judge/Special Judge, Anti-Corruption, Rawalpindi Division, Rawalpindi, is upheld.
(SYED FARHAD ALI SHAH)
